summary: Specifies the non-media data transport aspects of WebRTC, giving an architectural overview of how SCTP is used as a generic transport service so browsers can exchange non-media data directly.

plainLanguage.summary: A WebRTC call between two browsers carries voice and video. This document covers the other half: a way to send any kind of data between the two browsers, as if they were connected by a socket. The data travels inside an encrypted session, gets through firewalls and home routers, and is split into separate channels so that a stalled file transfer does not block the chat.

questions: how do webrtc data channels work
why does webrtc use sctp over dtls
what is the maximum webrtc data channel message size
subtitle: How browsers send arbitrary non-media data to each other: SCTP carried over DTLS over ICE/UDP.

tldr.problem: WebRTC lets two browsers exchange audio and video, but applications such as games, file transfer and text chat also need to send non-media data directly between peers, securely, through NATs and with congestion control.
tldr.mechanism: Data channels run over SCTP, which is encapsulated in DTLS over ICE/UDP. A data channel is a pair of SCTP streams, one in each direction, with the same stream identifier, with per-message choices of reliable or partially reliable and ordered or unordered delivery.
tldr.outcome: Browsers get WebSocket-like bidirectional channels that can share a single UDP port with the media, with confidentiality, integrity and source authentication from DTLS.

facts.label: Initial IP-layer path MTU
facts.value: SHOULD NOT exceed 1200 bytes (IPv4) or 1280 bytes (IPv6)

today: RFC 8831 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating document, so it remains the specification of the non-media data transport for WebRTC, with the in-band channel negotiation defined separately in RFC 8832.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
In the WebRTC framework, communication between the parties consists of media and non-media data. Media is sent using the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol and is not specified further here. Non-media data is handled by using the Stream Control Transmission Protocol encapsulated in DTLS. DTLS 1.0 is defined in one document, DTLS 1.2 in another, and DTLS 1.3 in an upcoming version.

The encapsulation of SCTP over DTLS over ICE/UDP provides a NAT traversal solution together with confidentiality, source authentication and integrity-protected transfers. This data transport service operates in parallel to the SRTP media transports, and all of them can eventually share a single UDP port number.

SCTP, as specified with the partial reliability extension and the additional policies, provides multiple streams natively with reliable, and the relevant partially reliable, delivery modes for user messages. Using the reconfiguration extension allows an increase in the number of streams during the lifetime of an SCTP association and allows individual SCTP streams to be reset. Using the stream scheduler extension allows the interleaving of large messages to avoid monopolization and adds support for prioritizing SCTP streams.
sections.plainLanguage: Three layers do the work. SCTP is a transport protocol like TCP but built for messages rather than a byte stream, and it can carry several independent streams at once. DTLS puts that inside an encrypted, authenticated session. ICE finds a path through whatever firewalls and routers are in the way. The whole thing can share the same UDP port as the audio and video.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.content:
This section lists the requirements for peer-to-peer data channels between two browsers. Multiple simultaneous data channels must be supported, and there may be zero or more SRTP media streams in parallel with the data channels in the same PeerConnection, with the number and state of those media streams changing at any time. Both reliable and unreliable data channels must be supported.

Data channels of a PeerConnection must be congestion controlled either individually, as a class, or in conjunction with the SRTP media streams of the PeerConnection. This ensures that data channels do not cause congestion problems for the media streams, and that the PeerConnection does not cause excessive problems when run in parallel with TCP connections. The application should be able to provide guidance as to the relative priority of each data channel relative to each other and relative to the SRTP media streams.

Data channels must be secured, which allows for confidentiality, integrity and source authentication. They must provide message fragmentation support such that IP-layer fragmentation can be avoided no matter how large a message the JavaScript application passes to be sent, and must ensure that large data channel transfers do not unduly delay traffic on other data channels.

The data channel transport protocol must not encode local IP addresses inside its protocol fields, because doing so reveals potentially private information and leads to failure if the address is depended upon. It should support unbounded-length messages at the application layer, such as an image file transfer, though implementations might enforce a reasonable message size limit. It should avoid IP fragmentation, must support path MTU discovery, and must not rely on ICMP or ICMPv6 being generated or being passed back, especially for path MTU discovery. It must be possible to implement the protocol stack in the user application space.
sections.plainLanguage: The list of requirements explains the design choices. Many channels at once, each reliable or not. Channels must not interfere with the media, so they are congestion controlled with it. The stack must work in a browser, which means it lives in user space and cannot rely on the operating system for anything.

sections.title: SCTP over DTLS over UDP
sections.content:
The important features of SCTP in the WebRTC context are TCP-friendly congestion control, modifiable congestion control for integration with the SRTP media stream congestion control, support of multiple unidirectional streams each providing its own notion of ordered message delivery, support of ordered and out-of-order message delivery, support of arbitrarily large user messages by providing fragmentation and reassembly, support of path MTU discovery, and support of reliable or partially reliable message transport.

The WebRTC data channel mechanism does not support SCTP multihoming. The SCTP layer will simply act as if it were running on a single-homed host, since that is the abstraction that the DTLS layer, a connection-oriented unreliable datagram service, exposes.

Each SCTP user message contains a Payload Protocol Identifier that is passed to SCTP by its upper layer on the sending side and provided to its upper layer on the receiving side. The PPID can be used to multiplex and demultiplex multiple upper layers over a single SCTP association. In the WebRTC context, the PPID is used to distinguish between UTF-8 encoded user data, binary-encoded user data and the Data Channel Establishment Protocol. The PPID is not accessible via the JavaScript API.

This stack has been chosen for three reasons: it supports the transmission of arbitrarily large user messages, it shares the DTLS connection with the SRTP media channels of the PeerConnection, and it provides privacy for the SCTP control information. Since DTLS is typically implemented in user application space, the SCTP stack also needs to be a user application space stack.

The ICE/UDP layer can handle IP address changes during a session without needing interaction with the DTLS and SCTP layers. However, SCTP SHOULD be notified when an address change has happened, in which case it SHOULD retest the path MTU and reset the congestion state to the initial state, setting the congestion window and slow-start threshold to their initial values. Incoming ICMP or ICMPv6 messages cannot be processed by the SCTP layer, since there is no way to identify the corresponding association, so SCTP MUST support performing path MTU discovery without relying on ICMP or ICMPv6, by using probing messages. The initial path MTU at the IP layer SHOULD NOT exceed 1200 bytes for IPv4 and 1280 bytes for IPv6.

SCTP provides congestion control on a per-association basis, so all SCTP streams within a single association share the same congestion window. Traffic not being sent over SCTP is not covered by SCTP congestion control.
sections.plainLanguage: The choice of stack buys three things: arbitrarily large messages, one encrypted connection shared with the media, and privacy for the control messages that set up the channels. Two consequences are worth noting. SCTP here acts as if it were on a single-homed host, because that is what the encrypted layer exposes. And because the browser cannot see ICMP errors, the path MTU has to be found by probing rather than by being told.

sections.title: Data Channel Definition and Properties
sections.content:
SCTP defines a stream as a unidirectional logical channel existing within an SCTP association to another endpoint. The streams are used to provide the notion of in-sequence delivery and for multiplexing. Each user message is sent on a particular stream, either ordered or unordered, and ordering is preserved only for ordered messages sent on the same stream.

Data channels are defined such that their accompanying application-level API can closely mirror the API for WebSockets, which implies bidirectional streams of data and a textual field called a label used to identify the meaning of the data channel. The realization of a data channel is a pair of one incoming stream and one outgoing SCTP stream having the same SCTP stream identifier. How these identifiers are selected is protocol and implementation dependent, and this is what allows bidirectional communication.

Each data channel has the following properties in each direction. Reliable or unreliable message transmission: in case of unreliable transmissions, the same level of unreliability is used; in SCTP this is a property of a user message and not of a stream. In-order or out-of-order message delivery for messages sent: again, in SCTP this is a property of a user message and not of a stream. A priority, which is a 2-byte unsigned integer; these priorities must be interpreted as weighted-fair-queuing scheduling priorities per the definition of the corresponding stream scheduler supporting interleaving, and for use in WebRTC the values used SHOULD be one of 128 for below normal, 256 for normal, 512 for high, or 1024 for extra high. An optional label. An optional protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: A data channel is really two SCTP streams with the same number, one in each direction, which is what makes it look like a bidirectional socket to the application. Each direction separately chooses whether messages are ordered and whether they are resent if lost, and carries a priority the scheduler uses to decide what goes first.

sections.title: Opening and Closing a Data Channel
sections.content:
Data channels can be opened by using negotiation within the SCTP association, called in-band negotiation, or by out-of-band negotiation, which is any method that results in an agreement as to the parameters of a channel and the creation thereof; the details are out of scope of this document, but applications using data channels need to use the negotiation methods consistently on both endpoints. A simple protocol for in-band negotiation is specified separately.

When one side wants to open a channel using out-of-band negotiation, it picks a stream. Unless otherwise defined or negotiated, the streams are picked based on the DTLS role: the client picks even stream identifiers and the server picks odd stream identifiers. The application is responsible for avoiding collisions with existing streams, and if it attempts to reuse a stream that is part of an existing data channel, the addition must fail. The application must ensure in an application-specific manner that the peer will also know the selected stream and the options for sending data from that side.

The SCTP association is set up when the two endpoints of the PeerConnection agree on opening it, as negotiated by the JavaScript Session Establishment Protocol, which is typically an exchange of the Session Description Protocol. It will use the DTLS connection selected via ICE, and typically this will be shared via BUNDLE or equivalent with the DTLS connections used to key the SRTP media streams. The number of streams negotiated during SCTP association setup SHOULD be 65535, which is the maximum number of streams that can be negotiated during the association setup.

SCTP supports two ways of terminating an association: a graceful one, where a procedure that ensures no messages are lost during the shutdown is used, and a non-graceful one, where one side can just abort the association. Each endpoint continuously supervises the reachability of its peer by monitoring the number of retransmissions of user messages and test messages, and in case of excessive retransmissions the association is terminated in a non-graceful way.

Closing of a data channel MUST be signaled by resetting the corresponding outgoing streams. If one side decides to close the data channel, it resets the corresponding outgoing stream; when the peer sees that an incoming stream was reset, it also resets its corresponding outgoing stream. Once this is completed, the data channel is closed. Resetting a stream sets its stream sequence numbers back to zero with a corresponding notification to the application layer, and streams are available for reuse after a reset has been performed.
sections.plainLanguage: Opening is either agreed inside the encrypted channel or agreed out of band by the application. Out of band, the two sides pick stream numbers by convention, the client taking even numbers and the server taking odd ones, so they do not collide. Closing is done by resetting the streams, which guarantees that messages already in flight are delivered or abandoned rather than lost, and the stream number becomes free again.

sections.title: Message Boundaries and Payload Identifiers
sections.content:
All data sent on a data channel in both directions MUST be sent over the underlying stream using the reliability defined when the data channel was opened, unless the options are changed or per-message options are specified by a higher level. The message orientation of SCTP is used to preserve the message boundaries of user messages, so senders MUST NOT put more than one application message into an SCTP user message. Unless the deprecated PPID-based fragmentation and reassembly is used, the sender MUST include exactly one application message in each SCTP user message.

Six PPIDs must be used. WebRTC String identifies a non-empty JavaScript string encoded in UTF-8, and WebRTC String Empty identifies an empty one. WebRTC Binary identifies non-empty JavaScript binary data, an ArrayBuffer, ArrayBufferView or Blob, and WebRTC Binary Empty identifies empty binary data. SCTP does not support the sending of empty user messages, so if an empty message has to be sent the appropriate empty PPID is used and an SCTP user message of one zero byte is sent; when receiving an SCTP user message with one of these PPIDs, the receiver MUST ignore the SCTP user message and process it as an empty message. The usage of the WebRTC String Partial and WebRTC Binary Partial PPIDs is deprecated; they were used for a PPID-based fragmentation and reassembly of user messages.

If a message with an unsupported PPID is received, or some error condition related to the received message is detected by the receiver, for example illegal ordering, the receiver SHOULD close the corresponding data channel. This implies that extensions using additional PPIDs cannot be used without prior negotiation.

The SCTP base protocol does not support the interleaving of user messages, so sending a large user message can monopolize the association. The message interleaving extension overcomes this limitation and SHOULD be used. As long as message interleaving is not supported, the sender SHOULD limit the maximum message size to 16 KB to avoid monopolization. It is recommended that the message size be kept within certain size bounds, as applications will not be able to support arbitrarily large single messages, and this limit has to be negotiated. The sender SHOULD disable the Nagle algorithm to minimize the latency.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message carries a small tag saying whether it is text, binary, or empty, so the receiving side knows how to interpret it. An empty message is a special case, because SCTP cannot send one, so it travels as a single zero byte with its own tag. The document also caps a single message at 16 KB when the sender cannot interleave messages, so one big message does not block the others.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document does not add any additional considerations to the ones given in the WebRTC security considerations and the WebRTC security architecture documents. It should be noted that a receiver must be prepared for a sender that tries to send arbitrarily large messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new here; the security of the whole mechanism is covered by the WebRTC security documents. The one practical warning is that a receiver has to cope with a sender that sends enormous messages.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
This document uses six already registered SCTP Payload Protocol Identifiers: DOMString Last, Binary Data Partial, Binary Data Last, DOMString Partial, WebRTC String Empty and WebRTC Binary Empty. The SCTP Payload Protocol Identifiers registry was created by the SCTP specification. IANA has updated the reference of these six assignments to point to this document and changed the names of the first four PPIDs, with the corresponding dates unchanged.

The six assignments now read: WebRTC String has value 51, WebRTC Binary Partial (deprecated) has value 52, WebRTC Binary has value 53, WebRTC String Partial (deprecated) has value 54, WebRTC String Empty has value 56, and WebRTC Binary Empty has value 57.
sections.plainLanguage: The six payload identifiers already existed in the SCTP registry under older names. This document renames four of them to the WebRTC names and points the registry entries at itself.

items.title: Reliable or unreliable
items.text: Whether a lost message is resent. The same level of unreliability is used throughout.

items.title: In order or out of order
items.text: Whether messages arrive in the order they were sent.

items.title: Priority
items.text: A 2-byte unsigned integer. The values used SHOULD be 128 for below normal, 256 for normal, 512 for high, or 1024 for extra high.

items.title: Label
items.text: An optional piece of text that identifies what the channel carries.

items.title: Protocol
items.text: An optional name for the sub-protocol running over the channel.
